Gauteng Maternal Health

By: Ntokozo Miya | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Following reports of a mother whose baby was decapitated during childbirth, we ask: just how safe are women seeking reproductive health services in Gauteng’s public hospitals?

Unique Selling Point:
2 of our 3 case studies share a record of their futile attempts to hold the hospitals and health department accountable for their ordeals. Their stories are a few years old however, they have videos of their recent sit-ins at the health department in February this year, and an audio recording of their February meeting with the MEC – which makes them quite relevant and current. They illustrate the difficulty many women face when trying to get the hospital to account for failed procedures. After many failed attempts to meet with the MEC and being sent from pillar to post, the ladies basically sat at the health department's reception for 3 days in a row, demanding to speak to the MEC.

Summary:
Following a gruesome and traumatic birth by a young mother at the Tambo Memorial Hospital during which her baby was allegedly decapitated, we explore horror stories from other women who sought help for birth and other reproductive health procedures in other Gauteng public hospitals.

Further information:
>Second to the Eastern Cape, Gauteng is one of the hardest-hit provinces by medical negligence claims arising from public hospitals, many of which are related to incidents in the obstetric and gynaecology ward. The province faced claims amounting nearly R22bil in the 2017-18 year.
>Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi acknowledges that some claims arise from incidents that happened years ago. For example, in our story, Bongie Msibi had her uterus removed without her consent in 2005 but it was in 2016 that she realised what had happened and that's only because then, she was trying to have another child.
>For years, since the dawn of democracy, the government has promised to make the women’s ward safer but seems to be failing to deliver on this promise and we must interrogate the ‘why’, at least in Gauteng where our case studies are based.

GAUTENG REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH SCRIPT - FINAL

VO - A Gauteng woman’s hopes to become a mother were crushed in the most horrific way at the Tambo Memorial Hospital in Boksburg last month.

During a difficult delivery, a mother tried to push her baby out but only the head came out. The rest of the baby’s mutilated body was left inside her for a few hours before it was removed.
LINK – The Gauteng province is second to the Eastern Cape when it comes to medical negligence claims, many of which arise from reproductive health facilities in state hospitals
VO – Last year, Gauteng was hit with nearly R22 billion in medical negligence claims.

For years, the province’s health department has struggled with the caseload relating to negligence.

Bongekile Msibi gave birth at the Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital in Soweto in 2005 but it wasn’t until 2016 that she realised there was a problem.
Bongekile Msibi

I was trying to conceive. I then went to a gynaecologist to confirm – I thought I had infertility problems only to learn that I did not have a uterus. When I went there to get answers to understand: was it necessary so that I can find closure and close this chapter and move on with my life.
VO – She says her uterus was removed at the hospital without her consent.
LINK – This is the kind of unfortunate narrative the United Nations wished to curb when its member states signed the Millennium Declaration in September 2000. - WE NEED TO ZOOM OUT THE TAMBO MEMORIAL HOSPITAL IN THIS LINK
VO – Member countries including South Africa resolved to work towards improving maternal health over the 15 years that followed.

In 2013, Katlego Mpyana gave birth at the Mamelodi Hospital in Pretoria. The medical professional who supervised the delivery did not give Katlego an anaesthetic, and at one point, left her unattended during the labour.
Katlego Mpyana

When she was trying to take out my placenta, I think it was attached to my uterus. It was just hard for her to pull it out. That’s when she tied the umbilical cord on her hand and then she pulled it so hard that the uterus came out.
VO – While Katlego was still in pain, during efforts to insert the uterus and manage the bleeding, a nurse brought an unexplained form into the room.
Katlego Mpyana

They held the paper for me and they also held the pen for me. I took the pen and wrote my name up there like I’m a 5-year-old.
VO – The hospital later told Katlego she had given consent to have her uterus removed.
Katlego Mpyana

It cannot be used a defence because a consent form was signed after they removed it. So how can I give you consent whereby you’ve already removed it.
VO – According to a Stats SA report in 2015, despite making progress, South Africa missed the UN’s maternal health targets such as improving the maternal mortality rate and proportion of births attended by skilled personnel.

Nurses union president Lerato Madumo-Gova says the shortage of skilled professionals in public hospitals has a direct impact on the rising number of negligence cases.
Lerato Madumo-Gova – Young Nurses Indaba Trade Union

You’ll find in a hospital where the ratio is supposed to be one is to one, by international standards ... But in our facilities you find that one midwife has to deliver 5 or more women at the same time. There is sometimes no advanced midwife that will then begin to know what to do if there if there is a complicated delivery.
VO - In 2015, the UN unveiled new goals including improving “access to quality essential healthcare services” and ending preventable deaths of newborns by 2030.

‘Thandi’ says her horrific ordeal began after delivering her baby girl at the Steve Biko Academic Hospital.
‘Thandi’

I knew that I had stitches, minor stitches. So what happened when I got home was, I felt I kept getting worse. I had an ooze coming out of my vagina. It was smelling awfully. I had nausea and headaches.
VO – When her baby was due for the seventh day check-up at a local clinic, ‘Thandi’ asked the nurse to also check on her stitches.
‘Thandi’

He had discovered a maternity pad inserted in my vagina of which I was not made aware of. I was stinking so badly because when they took it out, it was even turning green in colour.
VO - After being advised by a doctor to have her uterus removed following numerous procedures for fibroid growths, Debra Mtimkulu agreed to have the operation to reduce the risk of cancer. But things didn’t go as planned after the surgery in August last year.
Debra Mtimkulu

Whenever I drank liquids such as tea or water or juice it would leak. I told the doctor I have a problem. The doctor inserted forceps inside me and the liquid flooded out of me, from inside my vagina. It was not water coming out of me, it was urine. He said that during the operation he had either cut my kidney or my bladder by mistake.
VO – Debra’s life has not been the same since.
Debra Mtimkulu

I used my t-shirts and plastic bags to stop the leaking when I am among people. 01:12:55:07 – When I use diapers, I must also add 2 baby diapers and a plastic bag. I also wear two pairs of tights.
VO – She joined a support group started by Bongekile Msibi, for victims of medical negligence.

When Debra’s situation worsened, Bongie and Katlego, also a group member, staged 3-day sit-in at Gauteng health MEC Gwen Ramokgopa’s office.
Sit-in video with Bongie and Katlego

As you can see, that’s my breakfast, that’s my lunch and that’s my supper, and right there, right here is where the PA of the MEC sits.
VO – They demanded that the department act swiftly on corrective measures in Debra’s case.
Bongekile Msibi

All they did was give Debra just a pack of diapers. I had to go back again.
VO – There have been countless efforts by the nurses’ union to address concerns with the MEC.
Lerato Madumo-Gova – Young Nurses Indaba Trade Union

your enrolled nurses as well as enrolled nursing assistants are not being developed. They were once trained 30 years ago and they just left it there so they are just doing as they are seeing.
LINK – Considering the horror stories coming out of Gauteng’s public hospitals in recent months, can the province make a positive contribution to the country’s 2030 commitment?
VO – Gauteng health MEC Gwen Ramokgopa, who brought along her team of medical experts, says her department is urgently addressing the skills shortage.
Gwen Ramokgopa

We have put a lot of resources in skilling nurses and that is why we have midwifry, we also have advanced midwives to ensure that we provide the best care.
VO – She acknowledged the emotional scars of the women we spoke to, but would not be drawn to comment on the specific cases.
Gwen Ramokgopa

I don’t have that permission from the patients to discuss details with you.
VO – After years of not getting a response, when we made enquiries, all the women were suddenly required by the department to go to Charlotte Maxeke hospital.

On the day we met Debra, she was preparing to go there for the tests ordered by the MEC.
Claire comeback

02:00:17:05 – It is a coincidence that we bring the cases through to you and they happen to be seen in the week that we are also speaking to you, so what should she have done?

Gwen Ramokgopa

02:01:05:18 – The important thing is to present yourself to the health facility. 02:07:58:00 – My message to every patient is that: don’t leave any health facility without the facility manager having had an opportunity to rectify your concerns.

Claire comeback

02:05:06:00 – Debra did all of those things and more, and still nothing was done to help her so I don’t understand – did the department fail her?

Gwen Ramokgopa

If she had done that and she didn’t get support at the first instance when she presented herself, it means exactly that.
VO - Katlego Mpyana’s missing medical records resurfaced after Carte Blanche’s query into her case.
Gwen Ramokgopa

Unfortunately, you are interviewing me when the investigations that I have instituted are not as yet concluded and it may be ideal to allow me to conclude the investigations and respond.
VO - Ramokgopa says despite these cases, the province is making headway towards the 2030 target to provide “quality essential healthcare services”.
Gwen Ramokgopa

In terms of the programs that help women, we are sparing no effort to improve those services. We say our health facilities must provide the best experience possible, we’re striving towards that.
VO – Bongekile says the MEC’s response to their plight is indicative of how patients at public hospitals are treated.
Bongekile Msibi

It is assumed that you go to a public hospital – you are poor, you are not learned, you don’t know your rights and you don’t know what can be done and cannot be done. That mentality need to change. People need to be treated with respect and dignity.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: 2 of our 3 case studies share a record of their futile attempts to hold the hospitals and health department accountable for their ordeals. Their stories are a few years old however, they have videos of their recent sit-ins at the health department in February this year, and an audio recording of their February meeting with the MEC – which makes them quite relevant and current. They illustrate the difficulty many women face when trying to get the hospital to account for failed procedures. After many failed attempts to meet with the MEC and being sent from pillar to post, the ladies basically sat at the health department's reception for 3 days in a row, demanding to speak to the MEC.
metadata.Summary: Following a gruesome and traumatic birth by a young mother at the Tambo Memorial Hospital during which her baby was allegedly decapitated, we explore horror stories from other women who sought help for birth and other reproductive health procedures in other Gauteng public hospitals.
metadata.Further information: >Second to the Eastern Cape, Gauteng is one of the hardest-hit provinces by medical negligence claims arising from public hospitals, many of which are related to incidents in the obstetric and gynaecology ward. The province faced claims amounting nearly R22bil in the 2017-18 year. >Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi acknowledges that some claims arise from incidents that happened years ago. For example, in our story, Bongie Msibi had her uterus removed without her consent in 2005 but it was in 2016 that she realised what had happened and that's only because then, she was trying to have another child. >For years, since the dawn of democracy, the government has promised to make the women’s ward safer but seems to be failing to deliver on this promise and we must interrogate the ‘why’, at least in Gauteng where our case studies are based.
